name: git fetch
shortDescription: Download objects and refs from a remote repository without merging. It updates your remote-tracking branches while leaving your local branches untouched.
detailedDescription:
The `git fetch` command downloads new commits, branches, and tags from a remote repository but does NOT modify your working directory or current branch. It only updates the remote-tracking branches (like `origin/main`) so you can see what others have done.

This is the safe way to check for updates. Unlike `git pull` (which fetches AND merges), `git fetch` lets you review the incoming changes before integrating them. You can inspect the fetched commits with `git log origin/main` and then decide whether to merge, rebase, or ignore them.

Fetch is always safe to run — it never modifies your local work.

parameters.description: The remote to fetch from (e.g., 'origin'). If omitted, fetches from the configured default remote for the current branch.
Remove any remote-tracking branches that no longer exist on the remote. Essential for keeping your local branch list clean.
Fetch all tags from the remote, even those not reachable from the fetched branches.
Limit fetching to the specified number of commits from the tip of each branch.

examples.title: Fetch latest changes from origin
examples.description: Download what's new on the remote without affecting your local work.
examples.code:
git fetch origin

# Now see what's new on main:
git log main..origin/main --oneline

# If it looks good, merge:
git merge origin/main

examples.title: Fetch and prune deleted branches
examples.description: Clean up remote-tracking branches that were deleted on the server.
examples.code:
git fetch --prune

# Or configure auto-pruning globally:
git config --global fetch.prune true

examples.title: Fetch from all remotes
examples.description: When working with multiple remotes (e.g., origin + upstream in a fork).
examples.code:
git fetch --all

# Now both origin/* and upstream/* branches are updated

examples.title: Fetch a specific branch only
examples.description: Save bandwidth by only fetching the branch you care about.
examples.code:
git fetch origin feature-api

# Now origin/feature-api is updated

commonMistakes.text: `git fetch` NEVER modifies your local branches or working directory. It's always safe to run. If you want to also merge, use `git pull` (which is `fetch` + `merge`).
Without `--prune`, deleted remote branches leave stale tracking branches locally. Over time this clutters `git branch -a`. Set `git config --global fetch.prune true` to auto-clean.
Best practice: always `git fetch` first, review with `git log`, then manually merge or rebase. This gives you full control over what enters your branch.
